content: Royal Perth Hospital (RPH) is an 855-bed teaching hospital situated on the northeastern edge of the central business district of Perth, Western Australia. It also operates specialized rehabilitation facilities located at Shenton Park. History The origins of the hospital date back to June 1829, when the first colonial hospital was established in a tent on Garden Island, off the coast of Western Australia. By June 1830, the hospital tent was relocated to Cathedral Avenue in Perth. In 1833, a more substantial colonial hospital briefly operated from a rented room in a private house. In December 1840, the hospital reopened in a building that had previously served as stables, located at the corner of St Georges Terrace and Irwin Street. The hospital began operations at its current site on July 14, 1855, and was officially named the Colonial Hospital. Over the years, it underwent several name changes, being known as the Perth Public Hospital and the Perth Hospital, before being renamed Royal Perth Hospital in 1946. Future In 2005, the Western Australian Government announced plans to relocate RPH operations to a purpose-built facility in Murdoch, which will be known as the Fiona Stanley Hospital. Facilities Royal Perth Hospital is the largest hospital in Western Australia, employing over 6,000 staff and treating more than 70,000 patients annually. The hospital provides a wide range of services, including imaging services, cancer care, neurosciences, various surgical specialties, critical and emergency care, dermatology, internal medicine, hematology, and more. As a teaching hospital, RPH maintains close affiliations with Western Australia’s four major universities and TAFE institutions, offering practical and professional education opportunities. This ensures the hospital is staffed with well-trained and capable professionals. Additionally, RPH collaborates with other hospitals in the region, such as Sir Charles Gairdner Hospital, Fremantle Hospital, and Princess Margaret Children’s Hospital, to ensure comprehensive care for patients, even for services not directly provided by RPH. The hospital is also home to a leading Burns Unit, which develops advanced technologies to aid in the rehabilitation of burn victims. Research The Head of Research at Royal Perth Hospital is Professor Peter Leedman. The hospital is a leader in research focused on patient recovery and improvements in clinical practices. RPH shares its campus with several major research foundations, including the Western Australian Institute for Medical Research, facilitating numerous ongoing research projects. The hospital’s researchers contribute significantly to international scientific literature. In 1998 alone, RPH staff published 158 articles and 114 abstracts in peer-reviewed medical, nursing, and scientific journals. Additionally, they presented 190 papers at national and international professional conferences. Shenton Park The Royal Perth Rehabilitation Hospital at Shenton Park was originally established as an isolation tent hospital during a smallpox outbreak in April 1893. Over time, it became known by various names, including the Isolation Hospital, the Victoria Hospital, and the Infectious Diseases Branch, before finally being named the Royal Perth Rehabilitation Hospital. It played a significant role in the rehabilitation of polio patients following the epidemic of 1948–1956. Personalities Several renowned medical practitioners and researchers have worked at Royal Perth Hospital. Notable figures include Dr. Fiona Wood, recipient of the 2005 Australian of the Year Award, and Professors Barry Marshall and Dr. Robin Warren, who were awarded the 2005 Nobel Prize in Physiology. Their contributions have further enhanced the hospital’s prestigious reputation. The hospital’s motto is Servio, and its logo, introduced in 1935, is based on the arms of the City of Perth. The logo features the St. George’s Cross on a white shield with a black swan in the top left canton and a banner inscribed with the word Servio.
